extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, patent examiners, and patent attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on drafting and evaluating patent applications: how Claims, Specifications, Drawings, Models, and related parts must be prepared, what they may claim, and how the Patent Office will treat them. Focuses on design claims, improvement/generic/species claims, defects, and formal/illustrative requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim for a design: distinctness and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for a design must be as distinct and specific as a Claim for any other invention, if the nature of the design will permit. Nothing beyond the configuration or ornamentation, which constitutes the invention, must be mentioned in the Claim; neither the qualities of the substance upon which the design is imposed, nor the mechanical functions which the substance may thus be enabled to perform, being any part of the design itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Claim may be a verbal description of essential features or by reference to drawings indicating lines and figures. Different designs cannot be embraced in a single Claim; Claims for distinct designs cannot be joined unless so dependent as to come within usual joinder rules. Use of the phrase 'as shown and described' limits the patent to the exact design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim for an improvement: must distinguish from prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement is an invention essentially distinct from the original art or instrument to which it pertains; and a Claim for an improvement must, therefore, not only define the improvement, like any other new invention, but also fully and accurately distinguish between it and the old invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Claim should confine itself entirely to the characteristics of the improvement, embracing nothing not necessarily connected with it. If mention of features of the original is required for precise definition, the language must make clear those original features are not claimed. An applicant may be required to explicitly distinguish the old and new, but need not acknowledge the old as old in doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement claims cannot improperly broaden to original art
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for an improvement must be limited to the improvement itself and cannot be a Claim for the whole art or instrument when the advance is only an improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Claim that attempts to claim the whole original art as well as the improvement is invalid. Two or more distinct improvements cannot be joined in one Claim; if several associated improvements are claimed and one is old, the entire combined Claim may be void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement claim must show distinction in the Claim itself
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not sufficient that persons skilled in the art can distinguish the improvement from the original invention; the Claim itself must show it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Claim must demonstrate the distinguishing features by its terms (not rely solely on expert evidence). Fair construction may permit implied limitation, but the Claim language must indicate the improvement is what is claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic (genus) vs specific (species) claims: scope relations
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic invention represents essential characteristics of a group; a patent for the genus always covers the species. An invention consisting in the use of a class of substances for a certain purpose is generic as to the use of a particular substance of that class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A subsequent inventor of a species holds rights subject to generic inventor's rights; an inventor of a species may obtain a patent covering the genus unless another previously conceived the same fundamental idea and is using diligence in reducing it to practice. Generic claims do not cover different functions or results beyond their terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joining generic and specific claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an invention has only the common characteristics, its description supports only a generic Claim; if it also has special qualities, its description will support both specific and generic Claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both a generic and a specific Claim may be inserted where description supports both. The phrase 'substantially as described' in a Claim confines the Claim to the generic or specific invention described. Several species described under a genus does not permit aggregating separate specific Claims into one Claim to create a generic Claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific claim limits patent even if description is generic
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for a species limits the patent to that species, though the Description covers a generic invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specific Claim does not convert into a generic protection simply because the description is broader; specific wording governs scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a Claim is defective
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim is defective when it fails to define the real invention with sufficient completeness and precision, or when it claims more than belongs to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defective Claim that overreaches is absolutely void; defects may be remedied by re-issue, and overbroad Claims are also curable by disclaimer. Presence of a void Claim in a patent does not affect valid Claims unless there is evident intent to mislead or unreasonable delay in filing a disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office's settled Claim language determines validity and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The Claim is to define what the Patent Office, after due examination, has ascertained to be the real discovery of the inventor, and it must be amended or withdrawn according to the judgment of the officers to whom this duty is committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the PTO settles Claim terms by its decision, the courts will not disturb it or enlarge/narrow it by construction. The PTO has a duty to secure correct statement of Claims before allowing issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification signature and formal presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must be signed by the inventor, or by his executor or administrator, and the signature must be attested by two witnesses, each signing his full name, legibly written. The Description and Claims, and all amendments, must be written in a clear and readable hand on one side of the paper only; and all interlineations and erasures must be marked in marginal or foot notes on the same sheet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A wide left margin (legal-cap paper with numbered lines) is recommended. Signatures and attestations are formally required; under later statutes the drawing may be signed by inventor or authorized agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings, models, specimens: when required
rubrics_metrics.description: The law requires the applicant to furnish drawings, and a model or specimens, illustrating distinctive characteristics, whenever in the judgment of the Patent Office the case demands them. The requirement respecting drawings is positive where the nature of the invention permits; models/specimens are conditional upon order of the Commissioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature of the invention admits drawings, they must be filed; models and specimens only when ordered. The Commissioner's decision as to whether drawings or models are necessary and as to their sufficiency is conclusive except on proceedings to avoid the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings must correspond in essential characteristics with the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawings filed must correspond with the specification in all the essential characteristics of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings are another method of portraying the same invention; discrepancies between verbal and pictorial descriptions may create ambiguity rendering the patent void. Use reference figures/letters in drawings tied to the Description and Claims so verbal and pictorial representations illustrate each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings should supply the place of a model for simple inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawings filed must be so full and clear that, if the invention is a simple one, no model will be needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Patent Office requires drawings to, as far as possible, supply the place of a model because drawings circulate publicly. For complicated structures incapable of full plane representation, a model becomes necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing content rules for classes of inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings must exhibit every feature of the invention covered by the Claims. For an art, every stage or sub-process capable of illustration must be shown; in a machine or manufacture, disclose all essential parts in their proper places; the drawings of an improvement must exhibit the improvement itself disconnected and also sufficiently of the old structure to show connection; a design must be shown by drawing or photograph depicting all distinctive characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings need not be working-drawings nor on an operative scale. They are not intended as construction blueprints beyond showing essential attributes sufficient for a skilled mechanic to create and employ the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical/formal rules for drawings and their enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings must conform to rules prescribed by the Patent Office regarding size, materials, arrangement, and lettering, and must attain a uniform standard of excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules are rigorously enforced; until complied with the drawing is practically worthless and the application will not receive consideration. Drawings must be signed and attested by two witnesses with full legible names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model filing and model requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: A model is not required until the Patent Office orders it; when required, a model must clearly exhibit every feature of the invention which forms the subject of a Claim but should not include any other matter unless necessary for representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A working model is often desirable to enable examiners to understand operation. Models must be neatly and substantially made of durable material (metal preferred unless material is essential feature). Size, finish and other minor requisites correspond to PTO regulations; the sufficiency of a model is conclusively determined by the Commissioner. A model filed when not required is returned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model final disposition and relation to application filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a model does not constitute filing an application nor validate an imperfect Description or an improper Claim; each part of the application is judged by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an application is rejected and more than two years elapse, models may be returned on demand; upon formal abandonment the model will be restored; when a patent is granted the model remains in the PTO and cannot be removed except by authorized sworn employee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specimens for compositions of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Specimens, instead of drawings or model, are required in applications covering compositions of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Heading appears; full elaboration likely follows in next section.) The treatise indicates that for compositions of matter specimens are required in lieu of models/drawings when appropriate.
